identity.title: Position: Medical Large Language Model Benchmarks Should Prioritize Construct Validity

problem.claim: Determine whether medical LLM benchmarks measure the real-world clinical tasks they are intended to represent.

gap.claim: Existing medical benchmarks are often constructed from medical licensing-exam questions, creating a stated concern that leaderboard performance may not reflect real progress or the intended constructs.

contributions.claim: Argues that medical LLM benchmarks should and can be empirically evaluated for construct validity.
Connects LLM benchmarks with psychological tests and applies construct-validity frameworks as empirical foundations for benchmark validation.
Uses real-world clinical data in proof-of-concept experiments and proposes an ecosystem centered on valid medical benchmarks.

stated_novelty.claim: The paper introduces construct validity from psychological testing as an empirical lens for evaluating medical LLM benchmarks.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report proof-of-concept experiments using real-world clinical data that found significant gaps in the construct validity of popular medical LLM benchmarks.

narrative_sequence.summary: Medical LLMs make broad clinical-knowledge and physician-like-reasoning claims, commonly supported by competitive benchmark evaluations.
The paper questions whether leaderboard gains represent real progress because many benchmarks use arbitrarily constructed licensing-exam questions.
It defines construct validity as measuring the intended conceptual target and draws an analogy to psychological testing.
Proof-of-concept studies with clinical data report validity gaps, followed by a vision for valid-benchmark-centered evaluation.

source_observation.claim: The paper aligns broad evaluation claims with an explicit conceptual target and proposes empirical construct-validity checks using real-world clinical data.

lessons.interpretation: Evaluation is more informative when benchmark scores are tied to the real-world construct they are meant to represent.
lessons.application: Define the target capability before selecting a benchmark, then test the benchmark against relevant real-world data and report construct-validity evidence alongside scores.
lessons.exception: This move may be unsuitable when no credible operationalization of the target construct or appropriate real-world data exists.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the evaluated benchmarks, clinical datasets, construct-validity methods, metrics, or effect sizes.
The reported proof-of-concept findings are not detailed enough to assess their experimental conditions or scope.
